title: Sundial Analytics - Units Workshop & Tuning
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics (tokens/$), observed caching savings, and batching tradeoffs. Agreed to run two follow-on micro-benchmarks: KV-prefix cache test and 2x batch-size latency tail test. Action: Redwood to share updated pricing scenarios and a short benchmarking script; Sundial to provide representative prompt traces and target SLAs.
next_steps: Redwood: share pricing scenarios + sample benchmark script by 2026-08-03
Sundial: upload 24h prompt trace (anonymized) to shared S3 by 2026-08-02
Schedule follow-up 30m micro-benchmark review w/ SREs week of 2026-08-04
action_items: Evan Kim: send pricing spreadsheet with 'burst vs reserved' columns (due 2026-08-03)
Priya Shah: provide small python benchmark harness + README (due 2026-08-03)
Lena Ortiz: export prompt trace and remove PII then upload to shared bucket (due 2026-08-02)
Mark Rivers: confirm whether Sundial can run dedicated node tests in their staging by 2026-08-06
transcript:
[00:00:00] Evan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we've got 45 minutes on the calendar. quick round of intros then we'll jump into the tokens per dollar numbers and the two experiments we proposed.
[00:00:12] Lena: hi all, Lena here, we'll try to keep it tight, got to hop after 45.
[00:00:17] Priya: Priya from Redwood, I'll walk through the microbench results from last week and then suggest next steps.
[00:00:24] Mark: Mark, platform, looking for concrete numbers we can show to finance.
[00:00:28] Owen: Owen SRE, I'll be focused on the latency tail and infra limits.
[00:00:34] Cecilia: Cecilia from privacy, one quick question up front: anything in the bench that touches raw customer PII?
[00:00:40] Evan: Good call. No raw customer PII in Redwood's tests, we used synthetic traces. We'll rely on Sundial's anonymized upload for any representative test.
[00:00:47] Priya: Ok jumping to slide 3 — tokens/sec per dollar. We ran three configs: hosted small (gpt-like 7B), quantized medium, and a dedicated quantized 8-A100-equivalent pool. The headline: caching reduced token spend by roughly 18-28% on the conversational workload we saw.
[00:01:10] Mark: 18 to 28 percent is a wide band, what's driving the spread?
[00:01:14] Priya: It's prompt shape — sessions with short context and repeated system prompts get more benefit from prefix caching. Long multi-turn threads with lots of user changes get less. Also the KV cache hit rate varied between 52 and 74% across traces.
[00:01:30] Lena: our chatbots are often context heavy, we expect longer histories. So maybe we lean to batching instead?
[00:01:36] Priya: batching helps amortize compute, yes, but it raises tail latency — especially with CPU-to-GPU scheduling we saw 95th percentile latency jump from 110ms to 320ms at batch size 32 for the medium model.
[00:01:52] Owen: that's the risk — our SLAs ask for 200ms p95 for critical routes. We can't accept 320ms.
[00:01:58] Evan: Right, so tradeoff: tokens/$ vs latency. We recommended two paths last week: (A) keep smaller batch sizes + aggressive prefix caching + quantization, (B) larger batches on dedicated nodes for non-critical routes.
[00:02:12] Mark: can you quantify 'aggressive' caching?
[00:02:15] Priya: in our bench aggressive means keeping a 10k-token prefix cache per session and enabling full KV reuse where possible — that increased hit-rate by ~14 percentage points in the synthetic test. But on your trace it may differ.
[00:02:28] Lena: here's a dumb question, do we lose quality when we quantize that aggressively?
[00:02:32] Priya: small quality hits at int8/4-bit setups, for generation tasks we saw minimal semantic drift in our evals, but for code-completion-like prompts precision matters more. We should run evals on your prompts.
[00:02:44] Owen: about fallback and canaries — we had incidents before where cloud noisy-neighbor effects spiked latency. How does Redwood handle automatic fallback?
[00:02:51] Evan: We route by policy. If latency SLO breached on a host we can fallback to a cheaper, lower-latency model variant or another region. For private deployments we can also route to dedicated pool under the same account. There was a slight audio glitch in the recording here but the gist was routing policies and automatic graceful degradation.
[00:03:12] Mark: can you run two tests for us? One focused on prefix cache behavior using our traces, another looking at p95 tail with batch sizes 8, 16, 32 on dedicated staging.
[00:03:22] Priya: yes that's doable. We'll provide the harness. Expect results in ~3 business days after we get the traces.
[00:03:27] Lena: timeline is important, finance wants a projection by next Friday.
[00:03:31] Evan: We'll prioritize the pricing scenarios. We'll model units as tokens per dollar and tokens per second per dollar assuming your 95th p95 target.
[00:03:39] Cecilia: on security, we need KMS integration and audit logs; any further gaps?
[00:03:44] Evan: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and detailed audit logs. We'll share the SOC2 artifact and our KMS integration guide.
[00:03:52] Cecilia: great, please send the docs.
[00:03:55] Priya: going into bench details — we used a mix of streaming and non-streaming generation. Streaming reduces perceived latency but can increase total tokens billed in some cases depending on stop sequences. We instrumented cost per response both ways.
[00:04:10] Mark: curious about streaming causing extra tokens — can you give an example?
[00:04:15] Priya: sure — if you stream every token until a model emits a stop token and your client-side post-processing also re-requests or doesn't close the stream properly, you can double-read tokens. Also if you use aggressive sampling settings it can extend outputs. It's operational but common.
[00:04:31] Owen: SRE question — for the p95 tail test can we simulate cold KV caches vs warm caches? That will matter a lot.
[00:04:38] Priya: yes, we can instrument warm/warm-up windows and report hit-rate curves over time. We'll include cold-start numbers.
[00:04:44] Lena: on cost modeling — what assumptions do you make for active vs idle sessions? Our product keeps contexts for 48h by default.
[00:04:51] Priya: we modeled three retention windows: 30 min, 4 hours, 48 hours. Holding caches longer increases memory footprint but raises hit rates. We provide a memory-to-hit-rate curve so you can choose an operating point.
[00:05:02] Mark: can you walk quickly through the numbers you sent last night? I skimmed but didn't dig in.
[00:05:07] Evan: sure — slide 7 shows cost per 1M tokens across configs. For your workload synthetic estimate: hosted quantized ~ $1.9k, dedicated pooled (reserved) ~$1.2k with similar latency but requires commit. The caching scenario dropped the latter to about $900 when hit-rates were >65%.
[00:05:27] Mark: big delta. What assumptions on GPU utilization?
[00:05:30] Priya: we assumed 70-85% effective utilization on dedicated under steady load; hosted varies more due to multi-tenancy headroom. We'll share the utilization curves.
[00:05:38] Owen: is burst capacity priced differently? We need to know the marginal cost of spikes.
[00:05:42] Evan: yes burst is metered at a premium. We'll show both steady-state reserved pricing and burst pricing tiers in the spreadsheet.
[00:05:49] Lena: if caching gives us 25% savings but introduces complexity, what does the ops burden look like? Who maintains cache invalidation?
[00:05:57] Priya: Redwood manages cache lifecycle for hosted and dedicated. For Private you can opt for customer-managed cache with hooks. Cache invalidation strategies are policy-driven — TTLs, manual flush, or event-driven. We can instrument metrics for hit rate and eviction pressure.
[00:06:12] Mark: how safe is caching with sensitive prompts? Cecilia?
[00:06:16] Cecilia: we require that any cached data be encrypted at rest and access restricted, and PII never be stored in plaintext. If Redwood can guarantee KMS-wrapped cache keys and audit trail, we can consider it.
[00:06:26] Evan: we support KMS wrapping. We'll include a short note on encryption and retention for caches in the security doc we share.
[00:06:33] Priya: ok next, sample micro-benchmark plan: 1) KV prefix hit experiment using your anonymized trace, measure hit-rate and tokens saved, 2) p95 batch stress on dedicated staging nodes with batch sizes 8/16/32, collect 50,000 samples each, 3) quantization + streaming combo test for a subset of prompts.
[00:06:54] Mark: 50k samples each sounds fine, how long will that take to run?
[00:07:00] Priya: with dedicated staging available it should be a couple hours per config; queueing and data transfer could extend it to a day.
[00:07:06] Owen: do we need to spin up any infra or can Redwood run it on our behalf?
[00:07:10] Evan: Redwood can run them on hosted/dedicated staging, but if you want a private deployment test you'll need to run the harness in your staging. We can supply scripts.
[00:07:20] Lena: finance question - when you say tokens/$, are you modeling total cost including storage for caches and KMS operations?
[00:07:28] Priya: good point — our initial numbers were compute + model inference costs; we'll add estimated storage and KMS per-request costs to the spreadsheet for a full TCO view.
[00:07:37] Mark: in the spreadsheet please include two columns: projection with cache and without cache, and a sensitivity table showing hit-rate delta +/-10%.
[00:07:45] Evan: noted.
[00:07:47] Cecilia: there's one compliance ask — do you maintain audit logs for each inference call showing which model version produced the output?
[00:07:54] Evan: yes, we store model_version, request_id, route, and minimal metadata in audit logs. We'll share the log retention policy options.
[00:08:02] Priya: quick aside — we noticed a difference between seq-lengths in your public docs and the trace; the trace has longer system prompts than expected. That will reduce caching benefit.
[00:08:12] Lena: yes we recently added longer system context to improve persona, but maybe we can trim non-critical parts.
[00:08:18] Mark: let's flag that as optimization: persona compaction.
[00:08:21] Priya: ok we'll add persona compaction as an experiment: run evals with 3 compaction levels and measure hit-rate and user satisfaction (proxy via automated quality metric).
[00:08:33] Owen: on the batch tail test, will you report both p50/p95/p99 and service time distributions?
[00:08:38] Priya: yes distribution and breakdowns by CPU/GPU transfer times, kernel execution, queue wait.
[00:08:45] Evan: quick pause — any other blockers?
[00:08:48] Lena: only that we need the anonymized trace uploaded by Monday so finance gets numbers Friday.
[00:08:55] Evan: understood. We'll send the harness now, Priya will follow up with a short README.
[00:08:59] Priya: I'll also include a minimal docker-compose to run locally if you want to sanity check.
[00:09:05] Mark: perfect.
[00:09:07] Owen: one last ops note — if we run dedicated staging, what's expected cleanup after benchmarks? We don't want stale nodes.
[00:09:14] Evan: Redwood will tear down staging instances by default after bench completion unless you request persistent staging. We'll log the lifecycle events.
[00:09:21] Priya: wrapping up, checklist: 1) Lena upload trace, 2) Redwood send pricing + harness, 3) run micro-benchmarks, 4) follow-up meeting to review results.
[00:09:34] Lena: agreed.
[00:09:36] Cecilia: also please include SOC2 and KMS docs.
[00:09:39] Evan: will do.
[00:09:41] Mark: ok thanks everyone, we'll reconvene after the bench runs.
[00:09:46] Owen: thanks.
[00:09:48] Evan: thanks all, end.

Note: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings and shorthand; timestamps are intermittent (roughly every 10-90 seconds) and speaker labels sometimes approximate.
